stem: A73-year-old woman presents with worsening episodes of withdrawal and irritability. She has suffered from memory loss for some months. On examination, she is alert, fully oriented, displays good eye contact and normal psychomotor activity, but her short-term memory is poor and she has dificulty naming objects. Her score on the mini mental state examination is 20/30. She mislabels three of the numbers in the clock- drawing task. Her BP is 148/85, with pulse 70 and regular.The chest is clear, the abdomen soft and non- tender, and BMI of 22. Routine bloods are unremarkable, and a CT scan of the brain shows mild cerebral atrophy. What drug should be prescribed?
explanation: The picture here is consistent with Alzheimer's disease, with cerebral atrophy on CT scan and clinical.

stem: You are examining the performance of a new screening test for pancreatic carcinoma in patients presenting with epigastric pain and weight loss. It has a very high level of specificity. What does this mean?
options: The probability that patients with a positive screening test have pancreatic cancer is high
The probability that patients with a negative screening test do not have pancreatic cancer is high
The proportion of negatives that are correctly identified is high
The proportion of positives that are correctly identified is high
The proportion of negatives and positives that are correctly identified is high
explanation: Specificity (also called the true negative rate) measures the proportion of negatives that are correctly.

stem: A 62-year-old woman is reviewed in the rheumatology clinic. She has been managed in the clinic for some time with gradually deteriorating respiratory function due to pulmonary fibrosis, gastro-oesophageal reflux disease and Raynaud's phenomenon. Over the past few months she has developed increasingly painful proximal muscle weakness. On examination her BP is 128/82, with pulse 78 and regular. You can hear fine crackles on auscultation of the chest. There is obvious 4/5 proximal muscle weakness affecting the hip and shoulder girdle. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 109 g/l 115-155 g/L White Cell Count(WCC) 8.1×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets 201×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 140 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/l Potassium(K+) 4.9 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine 123 μmol/L 50-120 μmol/l Creatine Kinase(CK) 1121 IU/L 23-175 IU/L Which of the following autoantibodies is most likely to be positive?
explanation: Anti-Jo1 is present in approximately 20% of patients with myositis (the likely diagnosis here) and is seen.

stem: You are asked to review a 74-year-old woman in the Emergency Department who is currently being treated by her GP for a urinary tract infection with trimethoprim. She also has a history of hypertension for which she takes the combination of ramipril and indapamide. He has referred her in because of a rise of 30 in her creatinine. On examination her BP is 124/82 and there is no postural drop. Pulse is 70 and regular. The chest is clear. There is minor suprapubic tenderness, thought to be related to the UTI. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 129 g/l 115-155 g/l White Cell Count (WCC) 11.3×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets 203×10/L 150-400×10/L C-Reactive Protein(CRP) 88 mg/l 0-10 mg/L Sodium(Na+) 140 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium (K+) 4.5 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol Creatinine 152μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L Urea 7.1 mmol/L 2.5-6.5 mmol/L Which of the following is the most likely cause of the elevated creatinine?
explanation: Trimethoprim reduces secretion of creatinine in the proximal tubule,resulting in an increase in serum.

stem: A 17-year-old man is admitted to the Emergency Department following resuscitation after he suffered a cardiac arrest while playing soccer. He apparently gave no warning and collapsed on the soccer field. He was found to be in ventricular tachycardia and was defibrillated on the scene. According to relatives who accompanied him to the hospital, his father passed away suddenly from a cardiac arrest at the age of 42.On examination in the Emergency Department, his blood pressure is 122/82 mmHg and his pulse is 82 bpm and regular. His chest is clear, although he is complaining of soreness over his sternum. The ECG reveals a QT of 520 ms. What cardiac myocyte ion channel defect is most likely to be found in this patient?
explanation: Type 1 Long QT syndrome (LQT) accounts for 30-35% of cases of LQT, the most likely diagnosis here. It is.

stem: A 30-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department with progressive weight loss, night sweats and a chronic cough. He tells you he is feeling increasingly tired and is finding it hard to hold down his job as the administrator of a local charity. He has worked in a shipyard in previous years and smokes ten cigarettes per day. He has not travelled outside of the UK for several years though he was originally born and lived in the Philippines. He denies any history of tuberculosis or exposure to tuberculosis. On examination his BP is 122/80, with pulse 80 and regular. There is decreased air entry at the right lung base. The abdomen is soft and non-tender, and his BMI is 22. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 117 g/l 135-175 g/l White Cell Count(WCC) 11.9×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets 203×109/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 137 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium(K+) 4.5 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine 100 μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L C-Reactive Protein(CRP) 122 mg/L 0-10 mg/l hilar lymphadenopathy, patchy shadowing Chest X-Ray affecting the right upper and mid zones, small right pleural effusion Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Whilst patients may genuinely feel they have never been exposed to tuberculosis,migration from a country with high incidence is a significant risk factor-the Philippines has one of the highest in the world at 554/100,000 and over half of their population is under the age of 25.Moreover, the CXR changes suggestive of the condition and raised CRP,coupled with weight loss and night sweats make tuberculosis the most likely diagnosis. Mantoux and sputum testing are both reasonable next steps. Treatment can be started while awaiting culture results if suspicion of active disease is high, and PCR testing for TB is now also available from a number of centers.

stem: A52-year-old man comes to the Emergency Department with acute inflammatory arthropathy affecting his right big toe. He has been diagnosed with gout some seven months earlier and is currently taking allopurinol 200mg per day. You confirm an acute episode of gouty arthropathy. Which of the following cytokines is most associated with acute gout?
explanation: It is thought that acute episodes of gout are triggered by an increase in interleukin 1(IL-1), associated with hypertriglyceridaemia against a background of elevated urate. For this reason, IL-1 inhibitors such as canakinumab are used in the treatment of acute episodes.

stem: A 74-year-old woman is referred for post-mortem after dying suddenly at home. She had a history of Parkinson's disease and Lewy body dementia.You attend the post-mortem for teaching purposes. What do you expect to find as the main constituent of Lewy bodies?
explanation: Alpha-synuclein(AS) is a protein that is abundant in the human brain. It is found mainly in the pre-synaptic terminals of neurones; it is found in particularly high levels in the substantia nigra.Lewy bodies are aggregates of AS that occur in cells affected by Parkinson's disease.

stem: A 67-year-old woman is started on chewable calcium carbonate tablets by the staff in the Emergency Department having suffered a left Colles'fracture. She has a history of ischaemic heart disease, hypothyroidism and type ll diabetes and takes a number of medications. Which of these medications should she not take at the same time as the calcium carbonate tablets?
explanation: The efficacy of levothyroxine can be reduced by the concurrent use of calcium carbonate, due to decreased levothyroxine absorption. Administration of calcium carbonate and levothyroxine should be separated by at least 4 hours. Calcium salts may also decrease the absorption of iron, zinc and strontium ranelate and quinolone antibiotics.

stem: A74-year-old man comes to the clinic for review. He complains of persistent shortness of breath and ankle swelling despite being treated with ramipril, furosemide and bisoprolol fumarate for his cardiac failure. On examination, his blood pressure is 132/80mmHg;his pulse is 64bpm and regular. There are bilateral crackles at both lung bases, and pitting oedema of both ankles. You plan to add spironolactone to his regimen. Where is the primary site of action of spironolactone?
options: Proximal portion of the proximal convoluted tubule
Thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle
Distal portion of the proximal convoluted tubule
explanation: Spironolactone is a competitive inhibitor of aldosterone receptors found in the distal portion of the distal convoluted tubule; this drives great excretion of salt and water. Thiazide diuretics also act on the distal convoluted tubule via the sodium chloride symporter.

stem: A 26-year-old African-American woman comes to the Genetics Clinic with her husband who is of similar ethnicity. She has been identified as having haemoglobin genotype AS, or sickle cell trait. Which of the following haemoglobin genotypes in her husband mean that 75% of her offspring would suffer from sickle cell disease?
explanation: This is a situation where the carrier is a double heterozygote for haemoglobin(Hb) S and Hb C with intermediate clinical severity. This couple's offspring would therefore have a 25% chance of being SC,25% chance of being AS,25% chance of being AC and a 25% chance of being SS. Although SC and AC phenotype is milder than SS-they would have some clinical symptoms and propensity to sickling. Therefore,75% would have sickle phenotype.

stem: A 42-year-old woman presents to her GP complaining of a swelling on the left side of her neck. She has been suffering from night sweats and increasing aches and pains over the past few months which she thought were due to the menopause, and she has been treated with amoxicillin for a recent episode of pneumonia. She is a non-smoker who drinks three glasses of wine per week. On examination, she is pyrexial at 37.6℃;her blood pressure is 110/70 mmHg and she has a large left supraclavicular lymph node. Her chest appears clear on auscultation. She also has blue-tinged fingertips. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 104 g/l 115-155 g/L White Cell Count (WCC) 9.8×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets 182×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 138 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium(K+) 4.4 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine 110 μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L Erythrocyte Sedimentation Rate (ESR) 92 mm/h 0-10 mm in the 1st hour Cold agglutinins positive Which one of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Painless, slowly progressive peripheral lymphadenopathy is the most common clinical presentation of non- Hodgkin's lymphoma.The presence of peripheral cyanosis implies the presence of cold agglutinins. Lymph node excision or core biopsy is the investigation of choice because the architecture of the node is important in determining the prognosis.

stem: A 29-year-old man comes to the Emergency Department complaining of pleuritic chest pain. He has been suffering from a flu-like illness over the past 3 days and says that the chest pain is central, retrosternal and is relieved by sitting forward. On examination, his blood pressure is 125/72 mmHg;his pulse is 75 bpm and regular. There is a pericardial friction rub; there are no signs of left ventricular failure or consolidation on auscultation of the chest. What ECG changes would you classically expect in this situation?
explanation: This history and the finding of a pericardial friction rub are classical for a diagnosis of viral pericarditis, likely to be related to the flu-like illness described here. Concave or saddle-shaped ST elevation is well described, and elevated troponin or creatine kinase-MB is likely to be found. Rest accompanied by the use of non- steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs are the intervention of choice.

stem: You are asked to see a 72-year-old man who is recovering on the stroke ward having suffered a subarachnoid haemorrhage thought to be related to chronic hypertension. The nurses are noting wild fluctuations in body temperature and are concerned that this may be related to his brain haemorrhage. Which of the following areas is most likely to have been affected?
explanation: The anterior hypothalamic nucleus plays a crucial role in thermoregulation and circadian rhythms. It is situated at the inferior border of the paraventricular nucleus.

stem: You are telephoned by a local GP who is concerned about thyroid function test results for a patient who has become progressively more lethargic with marked weight gain over the past few months. Her thyroid- stimulating hormone is markedly elevated at 12.5mU/L,T3 and T4 are both below the lower limit of normal. You are asked to give advice about initiation of thyroxine replacement. In which situation is it most important to increase the thyroxine dose very gradually?
explanation: In the older population,the recommended initial dose of levothyroxine is 25μg once daily, adjusted in steps of 25μg every four weeks according to response. This is because of significantly increased risk of cardiac arrhythmia in older patients.

stem: A54-year-old man comes to the Cardiology Clinic for review some six weeks after discharge following an inferior ST elevation myocardial infarction. Current medication is bisoprolol fumarate, ramipril, atorvastatin, clopidogrel and aspirin. His main complaint is a constant, niggling,dry cough. On examination,his blood pressure is 122/82 mmHg; his pulse is 62 bpm and regular. His chest is clear and there is no evidence of peripheral oedema. His peak flow is 500 L/min (515L/min predicted). Which of the following is the most likely cause of his cough?
explanation: Angiotensin-converting enzyme(ACE) inhibitors interfere with the metabolism of bradykinin, leading to increased levels. Increased bradykinin is thought to drive the niggling,dry cough associated with ACE inhibitor use. Increased bradykinin is not seen in association with angiotensin II receptor blockers.

stem: A 25-year-old man explains that he has experienced episodes where he is unable to move just before onset of sleep, and just after waking. Each time it occurs it leaves him feeling frightened and anxious. It is sometimes associated with visual disturbances. He has no past medical history of note. Examination in the clinic reveals nil of note, with general physical and neurological assessments entirely normal. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Sleep paralysis is common, and is seen more frequently in younger versus older individuals. It is associated with poor sleep hygiene and, if patients are particularly troubled by it, they are encouraged to take measures such as fixing a sleep time and minimising consumption of alcohol and/or stimulants such as caffeine. It may rarely be associated with other more significant sleep disorders such as narcolepsy.

stem: A 19-year-old student is reviewed in the Emergency Department with increasing tiredness, lethargy, multiple small joint pains and a central, dull chest ache. He attended his GP a few days earlier and was diagnosed with a Streptococcus pyogenes throat infection. On examination, he is pyrexial 38.2°C.His blood pressure is 110/80 mmHg; his pulse is 79 bpm and regular. He has a pansystolic murmur that is loudest over the mitral area. His chest is clear and there is no ankle swelling. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 109 g/L 135-175 g/l White Cell Count(WCC) 11.2×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets 119×10/L 150-400×10/L C-Reactive Protein (CRP) 210 mg/L 0-10 mg/l Erythrocyte sedimentation rate(ESR) 78 mm/h 0-10 mm in the 1st hour Sodium (Na+) 138 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium (K+) 4.5 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine 95μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L Urine blood Protein ++ Echocardiography Mitral valve vegetations Which of the following is the most appropriate intervention?
explanation: Although acute endocarditis due to Streptococcus pyogenes infection is rare, it is reported, and standard intervention is with a combination of intravenous penicillin and gentamicin.

stem: A17-year-old girl who is in the first year of studying for A-levels comes to the Emergency Department having suffered a third seizure in the past 6 months. According to her mother she refused to attend medical services after the first two episodes. She has a good level of school attainment and there are apparently no problems at home. According to the mother she has always been clumsy in the morning, suffering from sudden jerks affecting her hands, leading to frequent spillage of drinks. Apparently the girl's father developed fits at a similar point in his life. Examination in the clinic, including neurological status, is unremarkable apart from minor clumsiness holding a pencil and a cup. Routine bloods are normal. Which of the following is the most likely cause of the seizure?
options: Partial epilepsy with secondary generalised seizures
explanation: Q. Answered Flagged The characteristic history for JME, with increasing morning clumsiness associated with the development of fits in the teenage years, points us to the diagnosis. The normal school attainment also steers us away from other causes of epilepsy associated with learning difficulties. JME is inherited in autosomal dominant fashion. Levetiracetam, lamotrigine and sodium valproate are all potential treatment options.

stem: A 62-year-old man presents with worsening breathlessness, confusion and headaches over the past few weeks. Over three months ago, he began to have progressive exertional dyspnoea, aching in both legs and pain in the left arm after only 50 yards of walking. He has also noted bleeding around his gum line when he cleans his teeth and intermittent blurred vision. He has a history of hypertension for which he takes lisinopril. He smokes ten cigarettes per day and uses an occasional salbutamol inhaler. On examination, his blood pressure is 155/90 mmHg: his pulse is 78 bpm and regular.You notice bruising and petechial haemorrhages over his arms and legs. Auscultation of the chest reveals crackles and wheeze consistent with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. He has palpable femoral and popliteal pulses. Investigations: Which one of the following is the most likely cause of his presentation? Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 100 g/l 135-175 g/l White Cell Count (WCC) 9.2×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets 132×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 139 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium(K+) 4.5 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine 132 μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L lgA 2.8 g/l 1.0-4.0 g/l IgG 7 g/l 5-16 g/l IgM 24 g/l 0.5-2.0 g/l Erythrocyte Sedimentation Rate(ESR) 90 mm/h 0-10 mm in the 1st hour
explanation: Waldenstrom's macroglobulinaemia is characterised by the marked increased in viscosity seen here and associated symptoms. The marked elevationin immunoglobulin M is characteristic of the condition. Bone marrow investigation in all symptomatic patients is advised to confirm the diagnosis. For patients with symptoms such as this man, a rituximab-based chemotherapy regimen is instituted. One commonly used triple combination option is rituximab with cyclophosphamide and dexamethasone.

stem: A74-year-old man is referred to the rheumatology clinic for review. He complains of joint pains that have increased over the past six months, particularly affecting his left shoulder and right hip. He takes ramipril and bendroflumethiazide to control his hypertension, simvastatin and aspirin 75mg. On examination, his blood pressure is 138/82 mmHg. His pulse is 70 bpm and regular. Heart sounds are normal, chest is clear, abdomen is soft and non-tender. There is obvious limitation of shoulder extension and abduction, and hip flexion. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 131 g/l 135-175 g/l White Cell Count (WCC) 7.0×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets 201×10/L 150-400×10/L Erythrocyte Sedimentation Rate(ESR) 15 mm/h 0-10 mm in the 1st hour Sodium(Na+) 140 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium(K+) 5.0 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine 100 μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L Calcium(Ca+) 2.3 mmol/L 2.20-2.60 mmol/L Alkaline Phosphatase 495 IU/L 30-130 IU/L Phosphate(PO-) 1.0 mmol/L 0.70-1.40 mmol/L Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Clues here towards Paget's include limited joint involvement, normal calcium and phosphate, and raised alkaline phosphatase, in the presence of normal renal function. Imaging is likely to reveal significant joint deformity related to abnormal bone remodelling. Treatment is with bisphosphonates.

stem: A 63-year-old man comes to the Cardiology Clinic some six weeks after an anterior myocardial infarction for which he received two stents. His current medication includes lisinopril, clopidogrel, aspirin, atorvastatin and bisoprolol fumarate. On examination, his blood pressure is 122/80 mmHg;his pulse is 72 bpm and regular. His chest is clear. His abdomen is soft and non-tender;there is mild pitting oedema affecting both ankles. He asks about his prognosis with respect to future cardiovascular events. Which of the following is most associated with a future risk of myocardial infarction if pertaining to this patient?
options: Consumption of five units per week of alcohol
explanation: Q. Answered Flagged Evidence of atherosclerosis affecting more than one vascular bed is strongly associated with a risk of future non-fatal cardiovascular events or cardiovascular death after myocardial infarction according to the REACH (Reduction of Atherothrombosis for Continued Health) registry. Other predictive risk factors include diabetes, smoking, low body mass index, history of atrial fibrillation and cardiac failure.

stem: A 27-year-old woman is prescribed oral montelukast to control her asthma due to increased shortness of breath despite maximised inhaled fluticasone propionate and salmeterol. Which of the following correctly reflects the mode of action of montelukast?
explanation: Montelukast is indicated in patients who are unable to achieve control of their asthma symptoms despite optimised inhaled corticosteroids and long-acting beta agonists. Montelukast blocks the cysteinyl leukotriene receptor 1 (CysLTR1), responsible for mediating the actions of the CysLTs, and found predominantly in the airway.

stem: A 41-year-old woman with a history of rheumatoid arthritis comes to the respiratory clinic with increasing shortness of breath, which was unrelieved by salbutamol and beclomethasone inhalers. She has no past respiratory medical history of note, and is a non-smoker. Medication for rheumatoid arthritis includes weekly methotrexate. On examination her BP is 122/82, with pulse 80 and regular. There are fine crackles on auscultation of the chest, and the abdomen is soft and non-tender with no masses. Investigations reveal an FVC 70% of that predicted (a fall of 15% since starting methotrexate therapy). Chest×-ray shows patchy shadowing. Which of the following is the most important intervention?
explanation: This woman has chest X-ray and pulmonary function tests that raise the possibility of methotrexate-related pulmonary fibrosis. In this situation methotrexate must be discontinued and oral corticosteroids initiated.

stem: A 42-year-old man who owns a bar in Spain has returned to the UK for the first time in 4 years. He has a 6- month history of polyuria, nocturia and joint pains, and has lost 10kg in weight. He also complains of loss of ibido which is causing significant problems in his relationship. He is a non-smoker who drinks six units of alcohol per week. On examination, he has increased skin pigmentation which he puts down to suntan, and hepatic enlargement on abdominal palpation, although he has no other stigmata of chronic liver disease. Investigations: What investigation is most likely to confirm the underlying diagnosis? Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 131 g/L 135-175 g/l White Cell Count(WCC) 6.9×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets 140×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 139 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium(K+) 4.5 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine 112 μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L Alanine aminotransferase (ALT) 34 IU/L 5-30 IU/L Alkaline phosphatase 190 IU/L 30-130 IU/L Gamma-Glutamyl transferase(YGT) 84 IU/L 5-30 IU/L Albumin 36 g/l 35-55 g/l Glucose 16 mmol/L 3.5-5.5 mmol/L Bilateral knee X-ray Chondrocalcinosis
explanation: The suspicion, with pigmentation, liver impairment, diabetes, and chondrocalcinosis, raises the possibility of haemochromatosis. Of the options given, transferrin saturation is the most useful initial investigation to confirm haemochromatosis, with a saturation of 45% or greater driving genetic mutation analysis looking for C282Y or H63D mutations.

stem: You are planning a procedure to insert a subclavian venous catheterinto a 72-year-old woman who presents with hypotension and urinary sepsis. She is of normal weight. Where is the optimal point of needle insertion?
options: 1 cm inferior to the junction of the middle and medial third of the clavicle
Superior to the clavicle at the deltopectoral groove
Just medial to the midclavicular line, with the needle perpendicular along the inferior lateral
Two finger breadths lateral to the angle of the clavicle
Two finger breadths inferior to the midclavicular line
explanation: The object is to cannulate the subclavian vein while minimising the risk of arterial puncture. This point of entry minimises the distance from the skin to the vein, and the chance of entering the pleural space.

stem: A 64-year-old man with proliferative diabetic retinopathy presents to the Emergency Department a few days after receiving intra-ocular anti-VEGF therapy in his left eye for proliferative diabetic retinopathy. He complains of a sudden deterioration in vision, swelling of both eyelids and an acutely red eye. He has a hypopyon, and slit lamp examination reveals severe inflammation in the anterior chamber. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: The temporal proximity of symptoms to the anti-VEGF injection raises the possibility of bacterial infection. Diagnosis with respect to the underlying bacteria is made by taking a sample of vitreous for culture. At the same time the entire vitreous may be removed to reduce the infectious load.

stem: A 70-year-old woman with a history of non-valvular atrial fibrillation is treated with rivaroxaban for stroke prevention. You are concerned that she may have poor compliance with her therapy. Which of the following is the best way to monitor rivaroxaban compliance?
explanation: Prothrombin time(PT) is influenced by rivaroxaban in a dose-dependent way with a close correlation to plasma concentrations(r=0.98). This makes it the optimal way to measure rivaroxaban compliance. International normalised ratiovalues are only relevant to coumarins.

stem: A 39-year-old woman who is treated with long-term lithium therapy for manic depressive disorder comes to the Endocrinology Clinic complaining of polyuria and polydipsia. She complains that she is drinking up to 51 of water per day and waking multiple times in the night to pass urine. On examination, her blood pressure is 125/82 mmHg, with a drop in systolic blood pressure of 20 mmHg on standing. Her body mass index is elevated at 32 kg/m.Routine blood testing reveals an elevated serum osmolality although urine osmolality is decreased. Which of the following is the most likely cause of her symptoms?
explanation: Q. Answered Flagged Diabetes Insipidus Media explanations Chronic lithium use is recognised to reduce both cAMP- and non-cAMP-related upregulation of aquaporin-2 gene expression. The role of aquaporin-2 is to drive reuptake of water from the urine, and the number of aquaporin-2 channels is increased in response to vasopressin. Blockade of the upregulation of aquaporin-2 gene expression reduces the effect of vasopressin causing nephrogenic diabetes insipidus.

stem: A30-year-old lady presents with joint pains that have been getting progressively more severe over the past 2 years or more. After clinical examination, blood tests and X-rays, she has been diagnosed with rheumatoid arthritis. Rheumatoid factor is negative and anti-CCP is positive. Hand X-rays show osteopenia and joint erosions. Her symptoms respond well to a course of oral corticosteroids. Which of the following is the poorest prognostic factor for rheumatoid progression in this patient?
explanation: In patients who are rheumatoid factor negative, anti-CCP positivity stratifies more rapid progression and more aggressive joint disease.

stem: A37-year-old woman comes to the Emergency Department for review. She has been suffering from fevers over the past few days and feels generally unwell. Her main complaint is of multiple erythematous macular lesions that resemble targets. She says these began first on the extensor surfaces of her arms and legs, but have now spread to involve the torso. Mucus membranes appear spared. Which of the following is the most likely cause?
explanation: Herpes simplex is the most common cause of erythema multiforme, the likely diagnosis here. The non- specific symptom of fever also fits with the diagnosis of a viral infection.

stem: A56-year-old man who has lymphadenopathy and splenomegaly has been diagnosed as having follicular B-cell non-Hodgkin's lymphoma. He is attending to begin therapy for the condition. Which of the following receptors is commonly targeted in the therapy for B-cell non-Hodgkin's lymphoma?
explanation: The CD20+receptor is found on the surface of B lymphocytes and is a target for immune therapies such as rituximab. By targeting the CD20+receptor, cells that express it are depleted. Because there are greater numbers of lymphoma cells, these are depleted most.

stem: A 21-year-old woman with a history of Turner syndrome comes to the Emergency Department complaining of exertional chest pain, shortness of breath and headaches that have worsened over the past few months. She has not engaged with medical services since her original diagnosis as her family have always had an aversion to medical interventions. On examination, her blood pressure is 155/90 mmHg in the right arm and 122/75mmHg in the left arm. She appears to have relatively weak femoral pulses. There is a loud systolic murmur in the left infraclavicular area. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Coarctation of the aorta is a common cardiovascular abnormality in patients with Turner syndrome; it is found in approximately 15% of patients. Bicuspid aortic valve is found in a similar proportion of patients. Elongation of the aortic arch is more commonly found,in approximately 30% of patients with Turner syndrome. The picture here with hypertension and differential blood pressures fits with coarctation as the underlying diagnosis.

stem: You are the consultant in charge of the hospital's Genetics Clinic and are consulted by a set of parents who have a child with significant congenital defects. The parents want to have a further child and are concerned that the disease may be inherited through the female lineage of the family.Given this history, you suspect there may be a mitochondrial inheritance pattern. Which one of the following features would be typical of a mitochondrial disorder?
explanation: Features of mitochondrial disorders include optic atrophy, neuropathy, diabetes mellitus, epilepsy, diabetes insipidus and sensory neural hearing loss. Mitochondrial dysfunction leads to deficiencies in energy production, which drives the mixed picture of neuronal and muscular dysfunction. Examples include DIDMOAD(Diabetes Insipidus, Diabetes Mellitus, Optic Atrophy, and Deafness) syndrome, Leber's hereditary optic atrophy, mitochondrial myopathy and Leigh syndrome.

stem: A 62-year-old man is reviewed on the ward a few days after suffering a right parietal lobe stroke. His blood pressure is now stable at 135/80 mmHg, his pulse is 75 bpm and regular. He is beginning to mobilise around the ward. Which of the following deficits is most likely to become apparent?
options: Deficit in understanding spoken and written language
explanation: Damage to the right parietal lobe leads to visual-spatial deficits that result in patients being unable to navigate around locations, especially places that are new to them, but also familiar locations.

stem: A 19-year-old man comes to the Haematology Clinic for review. He has suffered from increasing abdominal pain and fullness after a meal, and has intermittent jaundice that has progressed over the past two years. He tells you that his father and uncle had similar symptoms and both underwent a splenectomy. On examination his blood pressure is 110/70 mmHg; his pulse is 75 bpm and regular. His abdomen is soft and non-tender; there is obvious splenomegaly on palpation. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 92 g/L (spherocytes and increased 135-175 g/l reticulocytes seen on film) White Cell Count (WCC) 7.1×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets 203×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 140 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium (K+) 4.8 mmol/l 3.5-5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 90 μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L Alanine Aminotransferase(ALT) 23 IU/L 5-30 IU/L Albumin 40 g/l 35-55 g/L Bilirubin 25μmol/L 2-17 μmol/l Which of the following is the most appropriate intervention?
explanation: This patient has hereditary spherocytosis, an autosomal dominant condition. It results in progressive splenomegaly in some patients, which may lead to the symptoms of abdominal fullness seen here. Intermittent jaundice occurs as a result of haemolysis, which eventually increases the risk of gallstones. Splenectomy is therefore the treatment of choice for patients with severe symptoms.

stem: A45-year-old woman who is receiving cycles of chemotherapy for breast cancer comes to the Emergency Department complaining of a fever and a severe sore throat that has increased in severity over the past 24 hours. Sheis allergic to penicillin, having suffered an episode of anaphylaxis after taking amoxicillin some ten years earlier. On examination, she is pyrexial(38.8°C); her blood pressure is 100/70 mmHg and she is tachycardic with a pulse of 110 bpm. There is evidence of pharyngitis and she has an indwelling line for delivery of chemotherapy. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 88 g/l 115-155 g/l White Cell Count (WCC) 3.4(N O.2)×10/L 4-11×109/L Platelets 89×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium (Na+) 138 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium (K+) 4.5 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine 142 μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L C-Reactive Protein(CRP) 185 mg/l 0-10 mg/l Which of the following is the most appropriate intervention?
options: Ciprofloxacin and vancomycin with single dose gentamicin
explanation: Guidelines suggest that in high-risk neutropenic patients with sepsis of unknown origin (as it is the case here), combination therapy with ciprofloxacin and vancomycin is appropriate,accompanied by a single dose of gentamicin, where there is severe penicillin allergy.

stem: A 61-year-old man who is known to suffer from type 2 diabetes and hypertension comes to the Emergency Department with 30 minutes of central crushing chest pain. He has continued to smoke 30 cigarettes per day and is poorly compliant with his diabetes medication. On examination, his blood pressure is 90/60 mmHg; his pulse is 30 bpm and regular. His jugular venous pressure is elevated, his chest is clear and there is no ankle swelling. The ECG reveals complete heart block with inferior ST elevation. Which of the following arteries is most likely to be occluded?
explanation: In 60% of patients, the AV node is supplied by the right coronary artery, specifically the AV nodal branch artery.

stem: A71-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department with symptoms of a stroke. He has poor co- ordination affecting his left arm, and cannot sit up without falling to the left. He also has dizziness with a feeling of falling to the left,blurred vision and nystagmus. There is loss of pain and temperature sensation on the left side of the face and the right side of the body, and he has a hoarse voice. Where is the most likely site of the lesion?
explanation: The neurological features here are consistent with lateral medullary syndrome, which is caused by interruption of blood supply from the posterior inferior cerebellar artery. Because the small calibre of this artery does not lend itself to revascularisation,in occlusive stroke the only potential option is anti-platelet therapy and control of risk factors.

stem: A39-year-old woman comes to the Emergency Department complaining of an acutely painful left eye. She is currently undergoing treatment with methotrexate and rituximab for rheumatoid arthritis. On examination there is significant conjunctival injection. Fluoroscein staining reveals a dendritic corneal ulcer. Which of the following is the most appropriate intervention?
explanation: This woman probably has reactivation of a herpes simplex corneal ulcer as a result of her immunosuppressive treatment for rheumatoid arthritis. As such, topical anti-viral therapy with acyclovir is the most appropriate intervention.

stem: A 42-year-old woman comes to the Emergency Department having been punctured with a used needle after being threatened during a mugging. The perpetrator of the crime stated the needle had been used by an HIV positive person. She has no past medical history of note and the wound has been well irrigated after the event. Which of the following is the most important next intervention?
options: Test the patient for hepatitis B virus
Test the patient for hepatitis C virus
Test the needle for viral contamination
Vaccinate the patient against hepatitis B
explanation: With the proven effectiveness of HIV PEP,there is a strong rationale for starting the recommended combination of Truvada and Raltegravir, in total for 28 days of therapy. It is thought to be useful up to 72h after exposure. In a patient who has no significant past medical history there is little downside risk of treatment. BHIVA guidelines state that a sharps injury from index HIV positive individual should receive PEP, but that it would generally not be recommended if the index was of unknown HIV status.

stem: A 39-year-old Asian man who has recently moved to the UK comes to the Emergency Department with a rash affecting his shins (erythema nodosum). He says he has had it for a few weeks and has suffered from intermittent fevers for the past few months. He smokes 30 cigarettes per day and has a cough most mornings. On examination, his blood pressure is 122/82 mmHg;his pulse is 72 bpm and regular. He has an occasional wheeze on auscultation of the chest. His abdomen is soft and non-tender and his body mass index is 22 kg/m. Which of the following is the most important investigation?
explanation: In an Asian man with a history of chronic cough,fevers and erythema nodosum,it is most important to rule out tuberculosis. As such, a chest X-ray is the most important investigation from those listed. A sputum culture is also advised.

stem: A 56-year-old man with a history of hypertension comes to the Emergency Department with deteriorating vision. He has suffered from increasing headaches for the past 2 weeks which are unrelieved by paracetamol and ibuprofen, He admits to being poorly compliant with his anti-hypertensive medication. On examination his BP is 165/90, with pulse 75 and regular. He also has a left third nerve palsy. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: Unruptured internal carotid artery aneurysm can exert pressure on the oculomotor nerve leading to third nerve palsy. The other common lesion which can result in this deficit is a posterior communicating artery aneurysm.

stem: A51-year-old man comes to the Diabetes Clinic for review. Current therapy includes metformin 1.5 g total daily dose and pioglitazone 30 mg per day. He has a background of diabetic retinopathy and hypertension but is otherwise relatively free of complications related to his diabetes. On examination, his blood pressure is 132/82 mmHg;his pulse is 70 bpm and regular. His chest is clear. His abdomen is soft and non-tender; his body mass index is elevated at 31 kg/m. His creatinine is 122μmol/l and his HbAc is elevated at 63 mmol/mol.
explanation: Dipeptidyl peptidase-4 inhibition reduces the breakdown of endogenous incretin hormones such as glucagon-like peptide-1.This potentiates the incretin effect, improving insulin release in response to a glucose challenge and therefore glycated haemoglobin(HbA1c) control. The class also has minor positive effects on weight.

stem: A 67-year-old man with end-stage cirrhosis related to NASH comes to the Emergency Department with his wife. Over the past 48h he has become increasingly confused with a fever, and his abdomen has become increasingly tense and swollen. His ascites was last drained two months ago, and he received oesophageal banding for varices some three months ago.On examination his GCS is 13,BP is 105/80, and pulse is 88 and regular.His temperature is 38.2℃. There are obvious signs of chronic liver disease,including spider naevi and tense, painful ascites. He has bilateral pitting oedema of the legs. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 98 g/l 135-175 g/l White Cell Count (WCC) 12.4×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets 75×10/L 150-400×10/L International Normalised Ratio (INR) Sodium(Na+) 134 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium (K+) 3.4 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine 80 μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L Alanine aminotransferase (ALT) 112 IU/L 5-30 IU/L Alkaline phosphatase 192 IU/L 30-130 IU/L Bilirubin 29 mmol/L 2-17 μmol/L Albumin 22 g/L 35-55 g/L C-Reactive Protein (CRP) 182 mg/l 0-10 mg/l Which of the following is the most appropriate intervention?
explanation: This patient has spontaneous bacterial peritonitis, to which he is more susceptible as a result of his chronic liver disease. Given his decreased GCS, abdominal pain and marked elevation in CRP, IV therapy is indicated, with tazocin 4.5g TDS the preferred option.

stem: A72-year-old woman with a history of Type 2 diabetes and hypertension comes to the Emergency Department with confusion. Medication for hypertension includes amlodipine 5mg and bendroflumethiazide 5 mg; the dosage was apparently increased a few weeks earlier. On examination her BP is 152/82,with pulse 72 and regular. The chest is clear, there is no ankle swelling and the abdomen is soft and non-tender. BMI is 22. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 119 g/L 115-155 g/L White Cell Count (WCC) 7.1×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets 201×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 126 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Bicarbonate(HCO-) 29 mmol/L 24-30 mmol/L Potassium(K+) 3.4 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine 95μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L Which of the following is the most likely cause of her hyponatraemia?
options: Reduced sodium reabsorption in the thick ascending limb
explanation: The hyponatraemia here is almost certainly due to use of bendroflumethiazide. This causes increased distal tubular sodium loss, against a background of increased ADH, leading to increased water reabsorption against a background of excretion of urine excretion that is high in both sodium and potassium.

stem: A 28-year-old woman presents to the Endocrine Ward. She has symptoms of frequent near syncope, accompanied by sweating and tachycardia, and she claims her symptoms are only really relieved by eating carbohydrates. Because of snacking, her weight has increased by 5 kg over the past three months. On examination, her blood pressure is 110/72 mmHg; her pulse is 67 bpm and regular. Her chest is clear, and her abdomen is soft and non-tender. Her body mass index is 28 kg/m. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 121 g/L 115-155 g/L White Cell Count (WCC) 7.2×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets 201×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 139 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/l Potassium(K+) 4.4 mmol/L 3.5 mmol/L Creatinine 100 μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L Glucose 5.9 mmol/L 3.5-5.5 mmol/L Which of the following is the most useful next investigation?
options: Insulin, glucose and C-peptide during a 72-hour fast
explanation: Insulinoma explanations Although very rare, the suspicion here is of an insulinoma, and the optimal way to confirm the diagnosis is with a 3-day fast. Hypoglycaemia may be precipitated after an overnight fast and period of exercise, soin practice many patients who are admitted are given a period of exercise (eg on a static bike) each morning,to determine if symptoms can be precipitated.

stem: A74-year-old man is admitted to the Emergency Department from home after presenting with a worsening headache, neck stiffness and confusion over the past few days. He saw the GP some 4 days earlier and was prescribed amoxicillin for a respiratory tract infection, but his symptoms gradually deteriorated. On examination he is pyrexial with a temperature of 38.8℃, BP is 105/80 and pulse is 88 and regular. His GCS is 13, he has obvious pain on neck flexion consistent with severe meningism, and bilateral papilloedema on fundoscopy. You can hear signs of left basal consolidation on auscultation of his chest. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 131 g/l 135-175 g/l White Cell Count (WCC) 15.7×10/L 4-11×109/L Platelets 203×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 141 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium(K+) 4.3 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 102 μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L C-Reactive Protein (CRP) 204 mg/l 0-10 mg/l Which of the following is the most appropriate antibiotic choice?
explanation: The suspicion here is of pneumococcal meningitis, which is more common in the elderly. Versus N meningitides, where ceftriaxone alone is thought to be adequate, the combination of vancomycin and ceftriaxone is recommended to achieve better coverage and more rapid clearance of underlying bacteraemia.

stem: A19-year-old man comes to the Endocrine Clinic for review. He has been referred by the Emergency Department after taking an overdose that he describes as a cry for help', because he finds it difficult forming relationships and feels lonely. On examination, he is 1.9m in height. He is slim with a body mass index of 21 kg/m;he has sparse pubic and axillary hair and small, firm testes. Blood tests reveal a testosterone of 5.2 nmol/l and elevated luteinizing hormone and follicle-stimulating hormone. Which of the following is his most likely karyotype?
explanation: His symptoms are consistent with a diagnosis of Klinefelter syndrome with tall stature, sparse pubic and axillary hair and small, firm testes. The elevation in gonadotrophins with a testosterone below the normal range for males is typical of the condition. Around 90% of males with Klinefelter syndrome carry the XXY karyotype. Q. Answered Flagged AXY XY is incorrect. Given the phenotype here, the clinical picture is consistent with Klinefelter syndrome. AnXY karyotype with androgen resistance is of course associated with female external genitalia.

stem: A35-year-old man is referred for coroner's post-mortem after suffering a cardiac arrest while playing for his local pub soccer team. He had no previous cardiac history, took no regular medications, had a normal blood pressure according to his GP and his body mass index was 24 kg/m. Which of the following is the most likely cause of his death?
explanation: One-third of cases of sudden death in US athletes (from registry data) could be attributed to a particular cardiovascular cause. Where a cause was identified, 36% of cases were due to hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy.

stem: A71-year-old woman presents to the gastroenterology clinic for review. She has been referred by general medicine physicians having presented for the fourth time over the past six months with severe iron deficiency anaemia. She has had two upper Gl endoscopies and one colonoscopy,all of which have failed to demonstrate a source for the bleeding. Other past history of note includes Type 2 diabetes and hypertension. On examination her BP is 132/95 and there is an ejection systolic murmur, loudest in the aortic area. Her chest is clear. The abdomen is soft and non-tender with no palpable masses. PR is normal. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 99 g/l 115-155 g/l Mean Corpuscular Volume (MCV) 78 fl 76-98 fl White Cell Count (WCC) 6.1×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets 191×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 140 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium (K+) 4.3 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine 95μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L Alanine aminotransferase (ALT) 23 IU/L 5-30 IU/L Alkaline phosphatase 89 IU/L 30-130 IU/L Bilirubin 8μmol/L 2-17 μmol/L Albumin 40 g/l 35-55 g/l Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
explanation: In this situation with multiple normal upper endoscopies and a normal colonoscopy, there is little to be gained by repeating these. By contrast, capsule endoscopy may well reveal the source of bleeding. Small bowel angiodysplasia is a possible cause, which may be poorly visualised/inaccessible with conventional imaging. The presence of an aortic stenotic murmur raises the possibility of Heyde syndrome, where bleeding from angiodysplasia improves once the aortic valve is repaired.

stem: A72-year-old woman is admitted to the Emergency Department following a mixed overdose of tramadol and amitriptyline. She required support on the high-dependency unit for a period of 48h, and this is her second overdose over the previous six months. Which of the following is the greatest contributor to risk of future successful suicide?
options: Recent death of her husband (in the past year)
explanation: Bereavement is a significant risk factor for successful suicide. The highest suicide risk occurs among those never married, followed in descending order of risk by widowed, separated or divorced; married without children; and married with children. The recent death of her husband adds to feelings of hopelessness.

stem: A 46-year-old man comes to the Endocrine Clinic to discuss further tests to determine the cause of his weight gain, hypertension and dysglycaemia. He has gained three stones in weight over the last six months He has developed diabetes, which is currently managed with metformin, and hypertension, which is managed with three oral agents. On examination, his blood pressure is 155/90 mmHg; his pulse is 78 bpm and regular. He is obese, with a body mass index of 34kg/m.Urinary free cortisol is elevated on two separate 24-hour collections. Other blood tests are shown in the table. Investigations: Which of the following is the most practical test to differentiate between pituitary-dependent Cushing syndrome and ectopic adrenocorticotropic hormone production? Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 135 g/l 135-175 g/l White Cell Count (WCC) 7.1×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets 192×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium (Na+) 142 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium(K+) 3.7 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Bicarbonate(HCO) 31 mmol/L 24-30 mmol/L Creatinine 122μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L Glucose 8.4 mmol/L 3.5-5.5 mmol/L
explanation: The 8mg overnight dexamethasone suppression test and the 48-hour high-dose dexamethasone test may be useful when baseline adrenocorticotropic hormone(ACTH) levels are equivocal with regard to determining the cause of Cushing syndrome. Greater than 90% reduction in basal urinary free cortisol levels supports the diagnosis of pituitary-dependent Cushing syndrome; ectopic ACTH production is associated with lesser degrees of suppression.

stem: A 69-year-old man is referred to the neurology clinic with worsening symptoms over the past six months from a tremor and rigidity. He has found it increasingly difficult to walk to the local shop and has had to give up handwriting. He has a past history of hypertension and had a previous myocardial infarction some 8 years earlier. On examination you note rigidity and a resting tremor, worse on the right than the left. He has slowed voluntary movements, including reduced arm swing whilst walking, and stops when asked to cross a line painted on the floor. Which of the following initial therapies is most appropriate?
explanation: Q. AnsweredFlagged L-dopa and dopamine agonist therapy are both considered first-line options in the treatment of Parkinson's disease, the most likely diagnosis here. Some physicians institute a dopamine agonist as preferred choice in younger patients although there is little long-term evidence to support one option over the other.

stem: 2 )·:Y7 Lo Y1 A 25-year-old man presents to the Endocrine Clinic with a hard mass on the left side of his neck. This has enlarged gradually over the past three months. He has a family history of thyroid cancer, but has previously refused all efforts to persuade him to atttend screening. He takes no regular medication and has seen the doctor once in the past five years. On examination, his blood pressure is 155/90 mmHg; his pulse is 78 bpm and regular.You feel a 3-cm thyroid mass on the left side of his neck. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 130 g/l 135-175 g/l White Cell Count(WCC) 5.9×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets 201×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 139 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium(K+) 4.3 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine 100 μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L Corrected Calcium (Ca+) 2.84 mmol/L 2.20-2.60 mmol/L Phosphate(PO-) 0.7 mmol/L 0.70-1.40 mmol/L Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis with respect to his neck mass?
explanation: This patient is hypertensive and hypercalcaemic against a background of a familial thyroid cancer. Given all these features, multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2 with hyperparathyroidism, a phaeochromocytoma and possible medullary thyroid cancer fits with the scenario.Thyroidectomy is the only potential intervention, and other relatives in the family should be screened. A phaeochromocytoma must be excluded; if found, it should be appropriately managed with a blockers before surgery is considered.

stem: A 60-year-old man with chronic atrial fibrillation is treated with daily warfarin therapy. He has had two unprovoked tonic-clonic seizures that were witnessed by his wife. A brain CT shows only some diffuse ischaemic changes in the white matter. Neurological examination in the clinic is unremarkable. The GP asks about starting him on an antiepileptic drug. Which one of the following antiepileptic drugs does not have important drug interactions with warfarin?
explanation: Uridine 5'-diphospho-glucuronosyltransferases are responsible for the metabolism of lamotrigine; interactions with agents metabolised by the cytochrome P450 system are not usually seen.

stem: A36-year-old woman who is known to have SLE, currently treated with hydroxychloroquine, presents to the rheumatology clinic for review. Despite receiving hydroxychloroquine she still has persistent pain affecting a number of small joints, and a photosensitive rash affecting her face predominantly. Her main concern is that over the past few months she has developed progressive pitting oedema affecting both legs. On examination her BP is 148/85, with pulse 70 and regular. Heart sounds are normal,the chest is clear and you confirm pitting oedema of both legs. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 101 g/L 115-155 g/l White Cell Count(WCC) 8.3×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets 95×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 137 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium (K+) 5.0 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine 132μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L Albumin 24 g/l 35-55 g/l Alanine aminotransferase(ALT) 52 IU/L 5-30 IU/L Bilirubin 8 mmol/L 2-17μmol/L Urine blood Protein +++ Which of the following is the immunosuppressive therapy of choice in this situation?
explanation: This patient most likely has membranous nephropathy as a result of lupus nephritis, and given she has significant protein loss as exemplified by her symptoms and low serum albumin, intervention is warranted. KDIGO guidelines recommend mycophenolate as the initial intervention of choice.

stem: A52-year-old man comes to the rheumatology clinic for review. Despite taking allopurinol 300 mg per day, he suffered a third attack of acute gout in the past year some five weeks earlier, affecting his right knee. This settled with NSAIDs, but he is finding the episodes increasingly disabling with respect to continuing his job as a kitchen fitter. He has no other past medical history of note and has reduced his alcohol consumption from four pints of beer per day to six pints of beer per week. Examination in the clinic is unremarkable. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 130 g/l 135-175 g/l White Cell Count (WCC) 8.2×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets 203×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium (Na+) 140 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium (K+) 4.5 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine 123 μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L Uric acid 550 μmol/L 200-430 μmol/L You plan to start benzbromarone. What is its mode of action?
options: Inhibits uric acid reabsorption in the kidney
explanation: Benzbromarone is a URAT-1 inhibitor which increases the excretion of uric acid. In combination with a xanthine oxidase inhibitor, it further reduces serum uric acid and is therefore an option for patients who fail to achieve uric acid target/suffer further gout episodes despite maximal allopurinol therapy. It may lead to an increase in creatinine and/or increased risk of renal stones in some patients.

stem: A 67-year-old man comes to the Emergency Department with a marked increase in his shortness of breath over the past few days. He has a history of mild asthma for which he uses a salbutamol inhaler, and he smokes five cigarettes per day. He also has a history of hypertension for which he takes amlodipine,5 mg per day. On examination his BP is 152/89, with pulse 82 and regular. He has a soft ejection systolic murmur There are scattered crackles on auscultation of the chest and O saturation measured by pulse oximetry is 92% on air. The abdomen is soft and non-tender. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 109 g/l 135-175 g/l White Cell Count (WCC) 11.1×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets 203×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 141 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium(K+) 5.0 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine 167 μmol(up from 119 some six months earlier) 50-120 μmol/L Chest X-ray patchy shadowing affecting both lung fields TLCO significantly elevated Urine blood Protein ++ Which of the following is the most likely cause for his shortness of breath?
explanation: Clues here include the increased TLCO, consistent with blood in the alveolar space; elevated creatinine, blood and proteinuria; and patchy shadowing on CXR consistent with fluid accumulation. It is likely that pulmonary vasculitis is the underlying cause, so tissue biopsy should be carried out to confirm the diagnosis (either from the kidney or via bronchoscopy), and aggressive immunosuppression considered.

stem: A 67-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department with a severe unremitting headache which has worsened significantly over the past week. He has also become increasingly red in the face and is developing dilated veins over his arms and neck. He smokes 30 cigarettes per day and has a chronic cough, occasionally productive of bloody sputum over the past 6 months. On examination he has mild proptosis, and he has a plethoric face and dilated veins in his neck and over both arms. Both conjunctivae are engorged. On examination his BP is 155/90, with pulse 88 and regular. There is bilateral wheeze on auscultation of the chest. The abdomen is soft and non-tender. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 109 g/l 135-175 g/l White Cell Count (WCC) 12.1×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets 132×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 137 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium (K+) 4.5 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine 122 μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L Erythrocyte Sedimentation Rate 82 mm/h 0-10 mm in the 1st hour (ESR) Chest X-ray right hilar mass consistent with an underlying bronchial carcinoma Which of the following is the most appropriate intervention?
explanation: The most likely diagnosis is bronchial carcinoma with superior vena cava obstruction. Evidence suggests that endovascular stenting to relieve the obstruction achieves rapid resolution of symptoms and preserves the possibility of making a tissue diagnosis later. Stenting is supported by a NICE review.

stem: 2 ):· Lo Y A 58-year-old white man comes to the Emergency Department to get an opinion about starting antihypertensive medication after being recommended to start this therapy by his GP. His blood pressure has been consistently above 155/90 mmHg on the past three visits to the surgery, and is 160/95 mmHg in the Emergency Department. General physical examination is unremarkable, and his body mass index is 24 kg/m. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 135 g/l 135-175 g/l White Cell Count (WCC) 6.1×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets 189×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 140 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium(K+) 4.5 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine 95μmol/L 50-120 μmol/l Chest no focal leison,no signs of cardiac failure ECG normal sinus rhythm, no signs of previous infact Which of the following is the most appropriate intervention?
explanation: It is clear this patient should not have attended the Emergency Department, but NICE guidelines are clear that in patients older than 55 years or those of Afro-Caribbean origin, calcium channel antagonists are the preferred initial intervention.

stem: A52-year-old patient with a history of type 1 diabetes for the past 45 years presents to the clinic for review. He tells you that he is finding it increasingly difficult to manage his blood sugars because of persistent vomiting after meals. He says it is unpredictable and sometimes he can vomit undigested food up to 2h after eating. He takes a basal bolus insulin regimen and his HbA1c has been below 8.5%(69 mmol/mol) over the past few years. He also has peripheral neuropathy and problems with postural hypotension. On examination, his BP is 122/82 and there is postural drop of 20 mmHg on standing. He is slim, with a BMI of 21, and you confirm that he has peripheral sensory neuropathy. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 121 g/l 135-175 g/l White Cell Count(WCC) 5.9×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets 201×109/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 140 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium(K+) 4.5 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/l Creatinine 112 μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L Which of the following is the most appropriate intervention for his vomiting in the long term?
explanation: Given the duration of Type 1 diabetes and presence of microvascular complications, it is likely this patient has diabetic gastroparesis. Interventions are targeted at reducing nausea and vomiting by a prokinetic mode of action. Domperidone is a dopamine antagonist that reduces nausea and promotes gastric emptying. Although it can raise prolactin levels, its profile is less adverse than metoclopramide for chronic therapy.

stem: A72-year-old Chinese man comes to the Emergency Department with a generalised, painful, blistering, erythematous rash. He saw his GP two weeks earlier with severe neuropathic pain across his upper chest following a bout of shingles, when he was prescribed oral carbamazepine. Other medication of note includes tramadol, lisinopril and amlodipine. On examination, he has a generalised maculopapular rash with extensive areas that have become necrotic and blistering. He has mucosal involvement leading to multiple blisters forming in the mouth. Which of the following is the most likely cause of the rash?
explanation: This patient presents with Stevens-Johnson syndrome (SJS), and given the proximity to recently starting carbamazepine therapy, this is the most likely cause. SJS is associated with HLA-B1502 positivity, and genotyping is recommended for patients of Chinese origin before starting carbamazepine.

stem: A 69-year-old woman presents to the neurology clinic with multiple episodes of pain affecting the left side of her face, below the eye. The episodes last from a few seconds to 2 min in duration, and she says they are sometimes triggered by cleaning her teeth or using a hair dryer when the air flow touches her face. She tells you that the pains are like an electric shock. Physical examination including neurological assessment is entirely normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate intervention?
explanation: The history here is typical for trigeminal neuralgia(TG). Carbamazepine has the most evidence for efficacy in treating TG and is therefore the correct option. New forms of the carbamazepine chemical series, such as oxycarbamazepine, do not have randomised controlled trial(RCT) data to support their use.

stem: A 42-year-old man presents to the Neurology Clinic for review.He has been suffering from headaches on most evenings during the past three months. He tells you they always affect the left side of his face and he last suffered from them about a year earlier, The headache occurs behind the eye, is sharp and penetrating in nature, is associated with tearing and redness of the eye, and lasts in total for 45-90 min. Up to two to three attacks can occur each day. On examination his BP is 122/80, with pulse is 67 bpm and regular. Neurological assessment is entirely normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate long-term intervention?
explanation: Q. Answered Flagged The history as described here fits with a diagnosis of cluster headache. Prophylaxis of choice is therefore verapamil, starting at a dose of 40 mg BD and slowly titrating it up to gain control of the headache. For acute episodes, oxygen therapy is effective and patients should be given a card to obtain O from an Emergency Department.

stem: A59-year-old woman who works in a cigarette factory comes to the respiratory clinic for review.She has progressive shortness of breath and wheeze, which has increased over the past 6 months despite having been prescribed a salbutamol and later a salmeterol inhaler by her GP.According to her husband, she coughs for some 15 min each morning. Other past history of note includes hypertension for which she takes indapamide. She smokes 30 cigarettes per day and has done so for 40 years. On examination her BP is 148/88,with pulse 78(atrial fibrillation). Chest expansion is reduced and there is wheeze with bilateral poor air entry on auscultation. She has pitting oedema of both ankles. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal Range Haemoglobin 131 g/l 115-155 g/l White Cell Count(WCC) 7.9×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets 181×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 141 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Potassium(K+) 4.5 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine 112μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L Chest X-ray bilateral hyper-expanded lung fields Peak Expiratory Flow Rate(PEFR) 270 (450 predicted) Which of the following is the most appropriate intervention?
explanation: Given the features on examination, chest×-Ray(CXR) and PEFR, the most likely diagnosis is chronic obstructive pulmonary disease(COPD). As such,from the options given, high-dose inhaled corticosteroid and LABA is the most effective intervention. This reduces exacerbations in clinical trials at the expense of an increase in events of pneumonia.

stem: You are asked by the nursing staff to review a 72-year-old man who is recovering on the orthopaedic ward after suffering a left femoral neck fracture. He complains that each evening people wearing brightly coloured clothes are standing outside his hospital room, and that there are geometric patterns painted on the wall at the end of his bed. The nurses tell you there is no one outside the window, and you can see that the wall is painted plain white. Neurological exam reveals that he is unable even to count fingers with either eye, although he can discern the blurred outline of your hand. Mini mental state score is 29/30.BP, pulse and temperature are normal. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation: CBS is associated with visual hallucinations as a result of significant visual impairment. Patients can complain of visual hallucinations featuring geometric patterns, or complex hallucinations involving objects or people, and these are more common as light begins to fade late in the evening. Patients should be reassured that their hallucinations are not real and that they can be ignored.

stem: A 45-year-old woman with a history of systemic sclerosis comes to the Emergency Department with a severe headache and tachycardia, coupled with feelings of extreme lethargy. She commenced a course of prednisolone for possible pulmonary fibrosis some 5 weeks previously. On admission her blood pressure is 165/95, with pulse 72 and regular. There are fine inspiratory crackles on auscultation of the chest. The abdomen is soft and non-tender, with no masses.You note sclerodactyly and peripheral calcinosis. Fundoscopy does not reveal evidence of papilloedema. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 101 g/L 115-155 g/L White Cell Count(WCC) 9.1×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets 152×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 141 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/L Bicarbonate(HCO) 21 mmol/L 24-30 mmol/L Potassium (K+) 4.9 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine 232 μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L Which of the following is the most appropriate intervention?
explanation: The clinical picture here, with marked hypertension against a background of steroid use, and deteriorating renal function, is consistent with scleroderma renal crisis. Management of choice is ACE inhibition, and if possible the steroid dose should be tapered/slowly withdrawn.

stem: You are asked to review a 54-year-old woman who is recovering on the surgical ward following a total thyroidectomy. She is very anxious and complaining of pins and needles in her hands, feet and around her mouth, and has had multiple episodes of carpopedal spasm. Her ionised calcium is measured at 0.75 mmol/L using the blood gas analyser. Her QT interval is 520 ms. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
explanation: This patient has acute symptomatic hypocalcaemia as a result of her thyroidectomy. She may have transient post-surgical hypoparathyroidism, but intervention is still essential because of her distress and the fact that she is at significant risk of cardiac arrhythmia.The ionised calcium is dangerously low at0.8mmol/L;1-2g of calcium gluconate is usually given over a period of ten minutes.

stem: A52-year-old man comes to the Emergency Department with a severe cough productive of rusty sputum; he also has a severe fever and has felt increasingly off his food over the past few days. He smokes five cigarettes per day and drinks no alcohol. He takes a salbutamol inhaler PRN for treatment of asthma. On examination his BP is 122/80, with pulse 90 and regular. His temperature is 38.9℃. He has a large cold sore on his right upper lip. Auscultation of the chest reveals signs of right-sided consolidation. Which of the following is the most likely underlying diagnosis?
explanation: S. pneumoniae is a common cause of community-acquired pneumonia,the most likely diagnosis here, and it is associated with reactivation of Herpes simplex-1 virus, leading to cold sores in up to 40% of cases.

stem: A 34-year-old man with a three-year history of ulcerative colitis is reviewed on the gastroenterology ward. He has been admitted three days earlier with an exacerbation of his UC, opening his bowels some eight to ten times per day with bloody diarrhoea. Despite IV corticosteroids there has been a relatively small impact on his symptoms, with bowels still open six to eight times per day and significant left-sided abdominal pain. On examination his BP is 105/80, with pulse 88 and regular. He complains of generalised abdominal pain particularly marked on the left side. Investigations: Investigation Result Normal Value Haemoglobin 100 g/l 135-175 g/l White Cell Count (WCC) 13.2×10/L 4-11×10/L Platelets 381×10/L 150-400×10/L Sodium(Na+) 141 mmol/L 135-145 mmol/l Potassium(K+) 3.4 mmol/L 3.5-5.0 mmol/L Creatinine 95μmol/L 50-120 μmol/L C-Reactive Protein(CRP) 210 mg/l 0-10 mg/l No significant improvement in either Abdominal x-ray colonic dilation or mucosal oedema Which of the following is the next appropriate intervention?
explanation: This is an effective salvage therapy for patients with severe refractory colitis and it has a rapid onset of action. It reduces the colectomy rate by 50% in the short term but its use is controversial over an extended period. For this reason other therapies such as azathioprine are substituted for the long term. Ciclosporin is administered IV in patients who do not achieve significant improvement after 72 h of corticosteroids.At this point patients should be placed under very close review;in the event of deterioration, surgery is the next step.
